i probably did about 100 a/b tests in different cases with speaker IDs/no speaker IDs and didn't find them to be beneficial in any significant way. that's my takeaway, that's my research.

So after a whole bunch of A/B testing I've found that I get *much* more consistent results for subjects speaking if I completely avoid using audio references. If I just say "<Subject 1> speaks in a light, British accent, saying <d>...</d>"... it just works. Add a reference according to the style guide, subject is babbling in at least 75% of the gens.

I've tried multiple variations. I think the model interprets the many occurences of 'audio' and pushes the subject to speak. For example you have a definition of the audio in `subject_definitions`, how the audio is supposed to be retained in `retention_analysis`, and then the subject is directed how to speak in `detailed_description` - I think the Qwen model picks up on those audio notes and says "well clearly the user wants the character to be speaking, a lot"

however ever since i dropped <Subject #> tags in lieu of <Character Name>, and started using time stamps for dialogue, and in a small capacity, describing what lips do before/after talking, the babble has been reduced 10-fold.
I tried timestamps - a lot of testing there - but the model will insist on having the character fill the silence before a timestamped dialogue reference, even if I say "lips closed", etc

If it's affecting the model's generation capacity, you should be testing prompt adherence and audio quality IMO. My original 2-pass was working flawlessly until I tried speakers. (At which point it failed horribly and I had to restart from scratch.) (But I'm not your dad, so please proceed as you like.)

So my limited testing on upscaling / cleanup suggests it's entirely possible provided:
- you can provide a quality first-frame. If you just give it a poor video and say "upscale" or "clean" this, it'll use the low-quality FF as a reference and hand it back to you
- you provide it with a detailed prompt so it can properly imagine the new detail. If you just say "upscale" or "clean" this, it'll use its own imagination as to what that means, rather than you guiding it to what it means

I'm made a test on scene consistency. I was having some weird issues with misalignment or a loss of spatial coherence, and so on. So, I tried something out.
I found the cause. The problem is [Shot1], [Shot2], [Shot3], etc.
If you want to maintain scene continuity, **STAY** in the same shot and indicate the timing for changes **within** that shot.
Left is the scene with shot 1,2,3, Right is just Shot 1

You should really only use "Shot" tags for major scene changes (a different location, a different scene, or an intentional cut); do not use them for camera angle changes—that is not what they are for.

> > [Shot 1] Tracking shot from behind of <Subject 2> walking quietly down the japanese alley in <Subject 1> on her way home from school. A beautiful sunset in the background. A gentle breeze stirs her hair and clothes delicately. The alley is empty and peaceful. at 00:04:00, the shot cut in a close-up  shot of the face of <Subject 2>. She kept walking, smiling happily, with the reflection of the sunset visible in her eyes and hair. at 00:07:00, the shot cut on a front full body shot of <Subject 2>, She's trying to adjust her hair with one hand.
I am providing part of the prompt so you have an idea of ​​how to handle the camera changes.

I'm beginning to wonder about the philosophy of prompting with minimax for longform cinematics/filmmaking. Is it better to go for longer clips that have 3 separate shots that are all related and can benefit from each others' contexts, but you have to wait longer times to see if the shot is actually following prompt/blocking/motion requirements for the scene... or is it better to just do short single shots and use lots of references to inform the model of previous shot compositions/scene context? I currently go for 10-15s gens, usually with 2-3 different shots. But it leads to long prompts that begin to confuse the model, and long wait times to find out if I'm getting "the one" ... the payoff is, if I do get it, I've just genned a big 12-15 second chunk of my short film which is huge. The pay off to the shorter shot philosophy is that the model will never be overwhelmed/confused by long prompts, and I'll be able to see if I'm getting good outcomes faster.. but that one's drawback is that it's more work to constantly be referencing your old scenes/shot blocking.
